title: Victim's family upset at probe pace
article: The family of Kevin St. Arnaud, a 29-year-old Vanderhoof man who was fatally shot by a Vanderhoof RCMP officer last December, said a year is too long to wait to find out how and why he died.
"It's been a very rough year for Kevin's family and my own. We have a lot of unanswered questions," Rebecca Gingera told media Monday on the anniversary of her common-law husband's death.

Flanked by her lawyer, Cameron Ward, Gingera, 28, said she has felt stone-walled by police whenever she has attempted to get information on the state of their investigation. That lack of communication has caused her to lose faith in the police force, she said.

"I believe that if they treat the victims of these situations with a little bit more respect and keep in touch with us a little bit more with the ongoing process, I think it might help," she said. "But all they do is slam the door on us. They shut us out and they don't give us any answers."
"I personally don't feel safe having the RCMP patrol the community because they are allowed to kill people and go back to work the next day," Gingera added.

Ward -- a Vancouver lawyer who has represented several families whose relatives have died in confrontations with police, including Jeffrey Berg, who died after an altercation with a Vancouver police officer in 2000, and Robert Bagnell who died after being hit with a Taser by Vancouver police last summer -- said Monday it is "inhumane" and "unfair" of both police and the B.C. Coroners Service to make St. Arnaud's family wait for information in the case.

To date, he said, the family still knows very little about how St. Arnaud died. According to police information released at the time of the shooting on Dec. 19, 2004, St. Arnaud had been pursued by a police officer in connection with a break-and-enter at a Vanderhoof drug store around 1 a.m.

Police said St. Arnaud, who was not armed, continued to approach the lone officer, even after he'd been warned to stop. He was facing the officer when he was shot three times from a distance of approximately five metres, and pronounced dead at the scene.

Both Ward and Gingera refused to discuss St. Arnaud's connection to the break-and-enter. Ward said those details remain part of the police investigation. He said just how St. Arnaud came to be in a confrontation with police is still "largely guess work."

Gingera said St. Arnaud had some problems with police when he was younger. But the man she knew, she said, was a hard worker, a talented artist, a gentle and kind partner and a good father to his two children, now age six and seven years.

Ward called for a coroner's inquest in the case so that some of those questions are answered. Ward said he has written to the solicitor-general's office in an effort to press that case, but has, to date, received no reply.

Ward has also requested that a special prosecutor be assigned to review the police investigation of the shooting. That request was turned down because it did not meet necessary criteria, said Stan Lowe, spokesman for the provincial Crown.
Lowe said special prosecutors are appointed in cases where there is significant risk of real or perceived interference with the duties of the Crown's office.

Lowe said the RCMP investigation into the shooting wrapped up Sept. 12 and senior Crown lawyers in Kamloops are currently reviewing file to determine if it meets provincial charge-approval standards. The case will then be handed over to senior Crown lawyers in Victoria for a separate review before a decision in made to lay criminal charges. He said a decision is anticipated early in 2006.
"It's important for the public to understand that we engage in painstaking deliberation whenever we receive these files," Lowe said.

Coroner Shane DeMeyer said it is standard procedure to wait until the criminal process is over before a coroner's inquest can be held. An autopsy report detailing St. Arnaud's cause of death will be released to the family at the same time, he said.
The RCMP officer who shot St. Arnaud had two years' experience on the force. The officer was transferred to another detachment in B.C. and was not suspended, RCMP said.
